scenes.title: The Circle Money Travels: GDP
scenes.summary:
In micro, the story was one cafe's sales. In macro, all spending in a country forms one big circle.

Households spend, firms invest, and the government spends. Add what foreigners buy from us, minus what we buy from them. The total is GDP — the sum in the formula below. The circle keeps turning when 💰 money flowing in matches money leaking out.

For example, imagine 30 🧑 classmates each spend a 10,000-won allowance at the corner 🏪 snack bar every month. The owner buys ingredients with that money and drops the rest in a 🐷 piggy bank. Adding up everything the class spent gives the class its own tiny GDP.

scenes.title: One Shock, Three Schools
scenes.summary:
In micro, prices moved the moment they were out of line. In macro, how fast prices move is exactly what splits the schools.

A sudden drop in demand leaves output below where it should be. That shortfall is called a gap. Classical economists say prices fall at once and close it. Keynes said prices freeze, so the gap just stays. New Keynesians say prices crawl, so the gap shrinks little by little. The only difference is the speed in the formula below.

For example, say a 🏪 snack bar raises its prices and 🧑 customers vanish overnight. One owner cuts prices again the very next day. Another cannot be bothered reprinting the menu and leaves them for months. A third lowers them a little each week. Customers come back at a different speed for each owner.

scenes.title: Why Aggregate Demand Slopes Down
scenes.summary:
In micro, demand curves slope down because buyers switch to the cheaper good. In macro, aggregate demand has nothing to switch to. All prices move together instead.

When the whole price level falls, the 💰 money in your wallet buys more. Feeling richer, people spend more. Interest rates also fall, so borrowing gets cheaper. 🧑 Foreigners buy more of our goods too. Together, these three paths raise spending. When the central bank prints more money, the whole curve itself shifts right.

For example, imagine every price at the corner 🏪 shop drops to half overnight. Your allowance stays the same, but it now buys twice as many 🍬 candies. You and your classmates all buy more than before. Nobody switched shops — every wallet simply got twice as fat.

scenes.title: After the Shock
scenes.summary:
In micro, a supply curve is drawn along costs. In macro, short-run supply hangs on the prices people expected.

When prices turn out higher than expected, 🏪 shops happily produce more. Once expectations catch up, output returns to its normal place. A demand shock ends up raising only prices over time. A supply shock, like pricier 🛢️ oil, cuts output and raises prices together. As the shock fades, the economy slowly finds its way back.

For example, a snack bar 🧑 owner expects plates to sell at 3,000 won and stocks up for a normal week. A festival suddenly floods the shop, so the owner cooks late into the night. Next year the owner plans for higher prices from the start, and output is back to normal. After the busy spell, only the higher prices remain.

scenes.title: The Multiplier: Spending That Echoes
scenes.summary:
In micro, the link from my spending to your income stays invisible. In macro, that link is what moves the whole economy.

When the government pays to build a bridge, the 🧑 workers earn income. They spend most of what they earn. That spending becomes someone else's income. So spending echoes around and grows bigger than it started. The more of each won people spend, the bigger the echo. That growth factor is the multiplier in the formula below.

For example, say you spend 1,000 won on snacks at the corner 🏪 shop. The owner uses that 💰 money to buy supplies next door. The next owner spends it again somewhere else. Your 1,000 won travels around the neighborhood, getting spent again and again. The neighborhood earns far more than your first 1,000 won.
scenes.chapterTitle: 3. Spending, the Multiplier, and the Paradox of Thrift

scenes.title: The Paradox of Thrift: When Everyone Saves, No One Does
scenes.summary:
In micro, a household that tightens its belt really does save more. In macro, when every household tightens at once, the story flips.

When everyone closes their wallet, 🏪 shops sell less. When shops sell less, 🧑 workers earn less. And when income falls, there is less 💰 money left to save. The plan to save ends up blocking saving itself. What is true for one household turns false for all of them together.

For example, say all 30 classmates stop visiting the snack bar to save their allowances. The owner earns nothing and cuts orders from the supply shop. The supply shop struggles too. The classmates filled their 🐷 piggy banks, but the neighborhood as a whole saved no more than before.
scenes.chapterTitle: 3. Spending, the Multiplier, and the Paradox of Thrift

scenes.title: A Price Is a Ratio; the Price Level Is a Level
scenes.summary:
In micro, a price was an exchange ratio between two goods. In macro, the average of all prices — the price level — appears as its own object.

If only ☕ coffee gets pricier, the basket really changes. Shoppers shift toward what stayed cheap. But suppose every price and every paycheck double. What people buy stays exactly the same. Only the money handed over doubles.

For example, at the 🏪 stationery shop a ✏️ pencil costs 100 won and an eraser 200 won. If both prices double and your 💰 allowance doubles too, you can buy the very same set as before.

scenes.title: The Equation of Exchange and Neutrality
scenes.summary:
In micro, money barely appeared; barter ran the markets. In macro, money moves to the center.

Double the money and prices double too. The pile of real goods does not grow. As the equation below says, money only rescales the ruler. Inflation is money growth minus real growth.

For example, ten 🧑 classmates share ten 🍬 candies. If the 💰 paper money with candy pictures doubles, each candy just costs twice as much.

scenes.title: The Market for Saved Funds
scenes.summary:
In micro, the question was whether one person saves. In macro, the stage is a market where the whole country pools its saving.

The interest rate is the price of borrowed money. A higher rate coaxes out more saving. It also scares off borrowers who wanted to invest. Where the two meet, as the formulas below show, sits the equilibrium rate. A government deficit eats into the pool, pushes the rate up, and crowds private investment out.

For example, imagine all your classmates pool their 🐷 piggy-bank 💰 money in one box. If many friends want to borrow and money is scarce, the charge goes up. If the teacher borrows big first, less is left for everyone else.
scenes.chapterTitle: 5. Where the Interest Rate Is Decided

scenes.title: The Market for Money
scenes.summary:
In micro, money barely showed up at all. In Keynes's macro, the money market sets the interest rate.

People like holding money because it is handy. The more nervous they feel, the more they hold. The central bank fixes how much money exists. The rate settles where the two meet, as the formulas below show. Print more money, and the rate falls.

For example, the whole class together carries a fixed pile of 💰 cash. On field-trip day everyone wants to carry more, so cash gets scarce. Scarce cash means borrowing it costs more — a higher interest rate.
scenes.chapterTitle: 5. Where the Interest Rate Is Decided

scenes.title: The Two Faces of a Wage: One Firm vs the Whole Economy
scenes.summary:
In micro, a wage is a cost the firm pays. In macro, that same wage is also the household's income.

One firm that cuts wages can hire more people. But what if every firm cuts at once? Customers' wallets get thinner, and goods stop selling. In the end, the jobs themselves vanish. The formula below traces that chain.

For example, a corner 🏪 bakery that cuts 💵 pay can afford one more helper. But if every shop in town cuts pay, customers have less to spend and 🍞 bread stops selling. Then helper jobs disappear too.
scenes.chapterTitle: 6. The Two Faces of Wages, and Unemployment

scenes.title: Menu Costs: When Prices Won't Move
scenes.summary:
In micro, an out-of-place price moved at once. In macro, the cost of changing price tags holds prices still.

Changing a price means reprinting the menu. Shops hate that cost, so they put up with small losses. Only a shock past the threshold below makes them move. While prices stay frozen, sales and jobs take the hit instead.

For example, ✏️ pencils at the 🏪 stationery shop cost 500 won. Costs creep up a little, but the owner leaves the tag alone. Rewriting every tag is more trouble than the small loss. Instead, the shop simply stocks fewer pencils.
scenes.chapterTitle: 6. The Two Faces of Wages, and Unemployment

scenes.title: The Trade Balance Is Saving minus Investment
scenes.summary:
In micro, a tariff was a story about one import market. In macro, the whole country's saving and investment set the trade balance.

If saving beats investment, the leftover 💰 money flows abroad. If investment beats saving, the country borrows from abroad. The gap always matches, as in the formula below. A tariff moves neither saving nor investment. So the trade balance ends up right back where it started.

For example, say your classmates collect 100 🍬 candies. If they eat 70 and save 30, those 30 can be lent to the next class. If they want to eat 120, they must borrow 20 from next door. A country's trade works the same way: it is the gap between what is saved and what is spent.

scenes.title: The Exchange Rate Closes the Loop
scenes.summary:
In micro, the exchange rate was one price among many. In macro, it is the very price that adjusts to match the saving-investment gap.

When our 💰 money gets pricier, our goods get pricier too. Foreign buyers buy less, and net exports fall. The equilibrium rate is where net exports equal the saving-investment gap. The formula below finds that spot. When government borrowing widens a deficit, the currency rises and net exports worsen by exactly that much.

For example, imagine the corner 🏪 shop suddenly charges more for 🍬 candy. Shoppers drift to the shop next door, and the pricey shop sells less. A pricier currency works the same way. Foreign buyers drift away until exports fall enough to restore the balance.

scenes.title: A Country Cannot Grow on Machines Alone
scenes.summary:
In micro, one firm's production function settled that firm's choices. In macro, we add that function up to a whole country and run it for decades.

More ⚙️ machines raise output, but each one adds less. Worn-out machines, though, grow in a straight line with the pile. Growth stops where the two flows meet. That meeting point is the steady state in the formula below. Poor and rich countries both end up gathering at the same spot.

For example, picture a village that plants 🌱 seeds. At first, each extra seed makes the harvest jump. Once the field is crowded, extra seeds add only a little. Some seeds also rot every year. When new planting just matches the rotting, the harvest stops growing.

scenes.title: Where the Saving Rate Comes From
scenes.summary:
In micro, splitting consumption between two periods was decided once and finished. In macro, that choice repeats every period, linked to tomorrow again and again.

The saving rate is not a number handed down to anyone. Each household chooses how much to spend today and leave for tomorrow. A higher interest rate or more patience changes what gets left. The formula below adds today's satisfaction to tomorrow's value. Modern macro models run on exactly this rule.

For example, say you get 10,000 won of 💰 allowance. You could spend it all today. But picturing the toy you want tomorrow, you drop some into the 🐷 piggy bank. Weighing tomorrow's fun alongside today's is exactly how the formula thinks.

scenes.title: Expected Utility vs Expected Profit
scenes.summary:
In micro, one person's attitude to risk and one firm's choice were studied apart. In macro, those attitudes add up and move the whole economy.

People dislike shaky outcomes, so they buy insurance. Given the same average, they pick the sure thing. Firms read only average profit and take the riskier project. Splitting it among many shareholders shrinks the shakiness. The formulas below set the two yardsticks side by side. Everything here is risk, where the odds are known.

For example, say a coin flip decides your 💰 allowance. Heads pays 10,000 won, tails pays nothing. The average is 5,000 won, yet you might prefer a sure 4,500. The 500 you give up out of caution is just like an insurance premium.

scenes.title: When Uncertainty Becomes the Recession
scenes.summary:
In micro, uncertainty was one person's problem, shareable through insurance. In macro, when everyone is anxious at once, nobody is left to insure with.

Fear of losing a 💼 job tomorrow closes wallets today. When everyone saves at once, 🏪 shop sales fall and the economy cools. Firms, fearing bad news, also postpone big investments. No average has gotten any worse. A recession can start from anxiety alone.

For example, imagine all your classmates start saving their 💰 allowance. Each one is just bracing for a rainy day. But if nobody buys 🍬 candy, the shopkeeper orders less stock. Nothing bad has happened yet, and already the neighborhood has gone quiet.

terms.definition: The market value of all final goods and services produced inside a country in a period. By expenditure, GDP = C + I + G + NX.
How far actual output sits from potential output. A negative gap is a slump; a positive gap is overheating.
Total spending demanded at each price level. Unlike a micro demand curve, it slopes down because a lower price level raises real money balances, lowers interest rates, and depreciates the currency.
Total output supplied at each price level. Upward-sloping in the short run because some prices are sticky; vertical at potential output in the long run.
How many units of income one unit of spending creates. With marginal propensity to consume c, the government-spending multiplier is \frac{1}{1-c}.
When everyone tries to save more, incomes fall and actual saving does not rise — it can even fall. The classic fallacy of composition: a virtue for one household, a trap for all.
terms.sceneTitle: The Paradox of Thrift: When Everyone Saves, No One Does

terms.definition: The average level of prices overall. A micro price is an exchange ratio between two goods (a relative price); the price level is the ruler for nominal values themselves.
terms.sceneTitle: A Price Is a Ratio; the Price Level Is a Level

terms.definition: In the long run, the money supply changes only prices, not real output or employment. It follows from the quantity theory and pairs with short-run non-neutrality.
terms.sceneTitle: The Equation of Exchange and Neutrality

terms.definition: Starting from the identity MV = PY (money × velocity = price level × real output), the theory that long-run inflation comes from money growth.
terms.sceneTitle: The Equation of Exchange and Neutrality

terms.definition: The classical market that sets the interest rate: saving supplies funds, investment demands them, and the interest rate is the price of saved funds.
Government borrowing pushes the interest rate up and displaces private investment, as the deficit absorbs saving in the loanable funds market.
Keynes's theory of the interest rate: people hold money for transactions, precaution, and speculation, and the rate is set where money demand meets money supply.
The fixed cost of changing a price, named after reprinting restaurant menus. Small — but near the optimal price the loss from not adjusting is also small, so prices stick.
terms.sceneTitle: Menu Costs: When Prices Won't Move

terms.definition: Net exports always equal saving minus investment (NX = S - I). A trade deficit is therefore a saving-investment fact, not something a tariff can fix.
terms.sceneTitle: The Trade Balance Is Saving minus Investment

terms.definition: The exchange ratio between two countries' goods. It is the price that moves to keep the trade balance identity true — doing the adjusting that tariffs cannot.
terms.sceneTitle: The Exchange Rate Closes the Loop

terms.definition: In the Solow model, the capital stock where saving exactly offsets depreciation. Growth returns to zero there; only the level remains.
terms.sceneTitle: A Country Cannot Grow on Machines Alone

terms.definition: The core of dynamic programming: today's value splits into the payoff of today's choice plus the value of tomorrow, V(a) = \max [u(c) + \beta V(a')].
terms.sceneTitle: Where the Saving Rate Comes From

terms.definition: How a person evaluates a risky choice: by expected utility \sum p_i u(x_i), not expected money. A curved utility function is what creates risk aversion and the demand for insurance.
Extra saving held against an uncertain future income. It grows with uncertainty — and when everyone does it at once, aggregate demand falls and a slump can follow.

exercises.statement:
A small economy has consumption C = 250, investment I = 100, government spending G = 90, and net exports NX = -40.

Find GDP and the consumption share.

A demand shock sets the output gap to -5\%.

(1) In the Keynesian world, what is the gap after 10 periods?

(2) In the New Keynesian world, what are the gap and the price level (starting at 100) after 3 periods?

The money supply stays at M = 100, but the price level rises from P = 1 to P = 2.

How much does each of the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate channels cut aggregate demand, and what does Y become?

A bigger supply shock lifts the short-run supply curve by 3 (shock size 30).

Find the short-run equilibrium output and price level.

Then explain what happens to prices if the central bank expands aggregate demand to defend output, and what ultimately remains in the long run in this model.

In an economy with MPC c = 0.75, the government raises spending by 20.

Find the multiplier and the total rise in income, and also the cumulative rise after the first three rounds.
exercises.chapterTitle: 3. Spending, the Multiplier, and the Paradox of Thrift

exercises.statement:
In an economy where investment is income-sensitive (I = 20 + 0.1Y, c = 0.8, income currently 420), every household cuts its spending by 6.

What happens to income and to realized saving?
exercises.chapterTitle: 3. Spending, the Multiplier, and the Paradox of Thrift

exercises.statement:
In an economy with ☕ coffee at 2, 🍞 bread at 4, and pay of 100, the coffee price alone quadruples to 8.

Find coffee and bread consumption, the price index, and real income.

A country's money supply grows at 8\% a year, real output at 2\% a year, and velocity is constant.

(1) What is inflation?

(2) Where is the price level (starting at 100) after 5 years?

(3) What happens to real money balances?

Households raise base saving from S_0 = 40 to 50 at the same time as the government runs a deficit D = 20.

Compared with the starting state (S_0 = 40, D = 0), what happens to the interest rate and investment?
exercises.chapterTitle: 5. Where the Interest Rate Is Decided

exercises.statement:
While a boom lifts income from Y = 200 to 220, the central bank also raises the real money supply from M/P = 90 to 105.

(1) Where does the interest rate go from its starting 5\%?

(2) What happens to investment?
exercises.chapterTitle: 5. Where the Interest Rate Is Decided

exercises.statement:
The whole economy cuts wages by 3.

With MPC c = 0.6, find (1) the change in output and jobs, and (2) the final wage bill. (100 workers, output 15 each, starting wage 10.)
exercises.chapterTitle: 6. The Two Faces of Wages, and Unemployment

exercises.statement:
The menu cost is F = 8 and the profit hill is \pi = 100 - 2(p - p^*)^2.

(1) Where is the edge \delta^* of the inaction band?

(2) For shocks \delta = 1.5 and \delta = 2.5, what happens to the price and to volume?

(3) Among twelve firms drawing the scene's assorted shocks, how many keep their price?
exercises.chapterTitle: 6. The Two Faces of Wages, and Unemployment

exercises.statement:
The world interest rate falls from r^* = 5\% to r^* = 2\%.

In a small open economy with no saving or investment shifts, find S, I, and NX, and say whether the country is a lender or a borrower. (Saving is S = 60 + 8r^* and investment is I = 140 - 8r^*.)

A surplus country with net saving S - I = 20 slides to S - I = -20 on government deficits.

With the net-export schedule NX(\varepsilon) = 90 - 5\varepsilon: (1) how much does the exchange rate appreciate?

(2) how much do net exports change?

(3) would either answer change if a tariff had been imposed along the way?

In a Solow economy with depreciation \delta = 0.1, find steady-state consumption c^* = y^* - \delta k^* for saving rates s = 0.2, s = 0.4, and s = 0.8.

Does eating more in the steady state always follow from saving more?

A household with interest rate r = 0.04 and income y = 4 holds assets a = 10.

Find its optimal next-period assets for patience \beta = 0.80, 0.90, and 0.95, then find the smallest \beta (on a two-decimal grid) at which this household stops running its assets down.

You are handed, for free, a lottery ticket that pays 180 or 20 with equal probability (expected value 100).

With utility u(x) = \sqrt{x}, what is the smallest sure amount you would trade the ticket for?

Read as insurance against the loss instead, what are the fair premium and the maximum premium?

The job-loss probability has risen to 50\%.

(1) How much does the scene's household (income 100 today, 60 or 20 tomorrow, \beta = 0.9) save, and what is its consumption today? Compare with the no-risk case.

(2) For the scene's factory investment (cost 100, value tomorrow 110 \pm 12), does investing now or waiting win, and what is the option value of waiting?
